background.definition: Meningitis is a bacterial, viral or (rarely) fungal infection of leptomeninges and the subarachnoid space.

list.listitem: 0.05 new cases per 1000 persons per year for Neisseria meningitidis.
Up to 19% of patients who recover have permanent hearing loss, mental retardation, or other serious neurological sequelae.

A summary of 5 case series found that the most common bacterial causes of meningitis in adults were Strep pneumoniae (53%), N. meningitidis (27%), listeria monocytogenes (4%), Haemophilus influenzae (3%).
N. meningitidis is carried asymptomatically by 10% of the population
Other causes include Enteroviruses, Streptococcus agalactiae, Escherichia coli, Mycobacterium tuberculi, Cryptococcus neoformans, Candida albicans, and Coccidioides.

Caused by bacteria, virus, or rarely in immunosuppressed patients a fungal infection. Typically spread by respiratory secretions, it is not spread by casual contact or through the air. Average incubation period for S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis is 3 to 4 days (range 1-10 days).
Seasonal variation in incidence with winter and early spring being the most common seasons for N. meningitidis infection.
Patients with complement deficiencies of C5 and C9 are more susceptible to infection with N. meningitidis.
Patients without a spleen, whether from trauma or sickle cell anemia, are more susceptible to infection with S. pneumoniae.
ACIP recommends vaccination with a quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenACWY) for adolescents aged 11 to 12 years. A booster is recommended at age 16 years.A

ACIP also recommends vaccination with MenACWY for persons aged ≥ 2 months at increased risk for meningococcal disease caused by serogroups A, C, W, or Y. This includes persons with persistent complement component deficiencies; persons receiving a complement inhibitor (e.g., eculizumab or ravulizumab); persons with asplenia; persons living with HIV infection; microbiologists exposed to isolates of Neisseria meningitidis; persons in a meningococcal disease outbreak caused by serogroups A, C, W, or Y; persons who travel to or live in areas in which meningococcal disease is hyperendemic or epidemic; unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated first-year college students living in residence halls; and military recruits.A
A pentavalent vaccine that adds serogroup B is now available and may be used in place of the quadrivalent vaccine in persons 10 years and older when vaccination for meningitis B is also indicated.A
Chemoprophylaxis with rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone should only be offered to close contacts of a patient infected with N. meningitidis. A

Suspect meningitis in patients with fever, headache, nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness, neurologic symptoms, and/or altered consciousness. It is very unlikely in persons without fever, altered mental status and neck stiffness. C
Obtain a CBC, blood cultures, and CSF analysis for patients presenting with fever and headache, neck stiffness, and/or altered mental status. C
A positive CSF culture is the gold standard for diagnosis of bacterial meningitis. If culture and Gram statin are negative order PCR or immunochromatographic tests for specific pathogens. C
A CSF lactate more than 31.5 mg/dL (3.5 mmol/L) and a CSF to blood glucose ratio of less than 0.4 are both strong indicators of a bacterial source.C

list.listitem: The classic clinical triad for meningitis is fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. However, less than two-thirds of patients present with all 3 findings. On the other hand, the absence of all 3 of the classic clinical triad virtually eliminates meningitis as a diagnosis (sensitivity 99%-100%).
Most adults with meningitis present with headache, fever, nausea or vomiting, and photophobia.

A review of several case series in Europe found that headache, fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status and nausea/vomiting were most commonly reported. The triad of fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status was seen in between 41% and 51% in the four series reporting them.

Assessment of neck stiffness should be done by observing Kernig and Brudzinski signs and applying gentle forward flexion with patient in supine position. While very specific the Kernig and Brudzinski signs signs lack sensitivity and if normal cannot be relied upon to rule out meningitis.

The jolt accentuation test is done by having patient turn his head horizontally 2 to 3 times per second. If headache worsens, the test is positive. A negative test is good evidence against meningitis in adults but a positive test is not helpful.
A Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) less than 11 may be a predictor of bacterial or fungal meningitis; however assessment of the GCS should not delay empiric antibiotic or dexamethasone therapy.

Obtain a CBC, blood cultures (before antibiotics), and CSF analysis for patients presenting with clinically suspected meningitis (e.g. fever and headache, neck stiffness, and/or altered mental status). The analysis of cerebrospinal fluid should include WBC, glucose, Gram stain to include acid fast staining, culture to include fungi, and lactate.

Cranial imaging prior to lumbar puncture is recommended by European guidelines (2016) for the patients with focal neurologic deficits, new onset seizures, severely altered mental status (Glasgow Coma score < 10), or who are severely immunocompromised.
The CBC and blood cultures should be drawn prior to initiating antibiotic therapy. Blood cultures are positive in up to 75% of cases of bacterial meningitis.
When performing a lumbar puncture, the type of needle appears to have no effect, however reinserting the stylet results in fewer headaches.
A CSF Gram stain is a quick way to check for bacterial etiology and is diagnostic when positive, but a negative Gram stain does not rule out a pyogenic source.

A positive CSF culture is the gold standard for diagnosis of bacterial or fungal meningitis, but as with Gram stain a negative culture does not rule out bacterial meningitis. It is positive in 60% to 90% of adults with bacterial meningitis. PCR and potentially immunochromatographic testing for specific pathogens such as N. meningitidis is more sensitive than culture and is recommended when culture and Gram stain are negative.

A CSF lactate of more than 31.5 and a CSF to blood glucose ratio of less than 0.4 are strong predictors of bacterial etiology.Negative Gram stain and culture and a normal CSF glucose are strong evidence for a viral etiology.
If confirmation of aseptic meningitis and identification of the causative organism is necessary, real time PCR for enterovirus is available and is highly accurate.
CSF or blood procalcitonin may be a useful test to diagnose bacterial meningitis.

Limulus endotoxin assay is sensitive and specific for diagnosis of Gram negative bacterial meningitis but is not currently recommended by the Infectious Disease Society of America Practice Guideline Committee.

The "FOUR score" incorporates assessment of eye response, motor response, brainstem reflexes, and respiration to predict mortality in adults with community acquired meningitis. Each 1 point increase in the 16 point score was associated with a significant decrease in the likelihood of a favorable outcome (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.89).
See algorithm in .
If bacterial meningitis is suspected, immediately start empiric antibiotics. A

For adults 18 to 50 when sensitivity of S. pneumonia to penicillin is reduced, cefotaxime or ceftriaxone PLUS vancomycin or rifampicin are recommended. For adults > 50 years or any adult with risk factors for Listeria when sensitivity of S. pneumonia to penicillin is reduced, cefotaxime or ceftriaxone PLUS vancomycin or rifampicin PLUS amoxicillin/ampicillin/penicillin G are recommended.A
Administration of dexamethasone with initial antibiotic treatment is a treatment option. A
Starting maintenance fluid hydration reduces chance of neurologic sequelae. B
If aseptic meningitis is suspected, observation and supportive therapy are recommended. C
If bacterial meningitis is suspected, start antibiotics immediately after LP or after blood cultures if CT scan is needed before LP.

European guidelines (2016) recommend the following for initial empiric therapy: Adults 18 to 50 when sensitivity of S. pneumonia to penicillin is reduced: cefotaxime or ceftriaxone PLUS vancomycin or rifampicin. Adults 18 to 50 when S. pneumoniae are susceptible to penicillin: cefotaxime or ceftriaxone Adults >50 years or any adult with risk factors for Listeria when sensitivity of S. pneumonia to penicillin is reduced: cefotaxime or ceftriaxone PLUS vancomycin or rifampicin PLUS amoxicillin/ampicillin/penicillin G Adults >50 years or any adult with risk factors for Listeria when S. pneumoniae are susceptible to penicillin: Cefotaxime or ceftriaxone PLUS amoxicillin/ampicillin/penicillin G. IV dosing: ceftriaxone 2 g q12h or 4 g q24h; cefotaxime 2 g q4–6 h; vancomycin 10–20 mg/kg q8–12h to achieve serum trough concentrations of 15–20 μg/mL; rifampicin 300 mg q12 h; amoxicillin or ampicillin 2 g q4h

An individual RCT of 301 patients randomized them to 10 mg dexamethasone or placebo every 6 hours for 4 days, and found a significant reduction in mortality (7% vs 15%, p <0.05). However, meta-analyses failed to confirm this mortality benefit.

A Cochrane review of 25 studies with over 4000 patients concluded that corticosteroids do appear to improve hearing and neurologic outcomes, though. According to one guideline, clinicians have the option to administer dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg q6 hours for 2-4 days) with empiric antibiotics for suspected cases of bacterial meningitis in adults.
Dexamethasone should only be continued if gram positive diplococci are seen on Gram stain or S. pneumoniae in confirmed in blood or CSF cultures.
In addition, corticosteroids reduce mortality (NNT = 14; 95% CI, 21-389) and morbidity in HIV-negative patients with tuberculous meningitis.

Standard WHO recommended therapy for cryptococcal meningitis is amphotericin B deoxycholate (3 to 4 mg/kg/day) plus flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses) for 7 days, followed by fluconazole (1200 mg/day) for 7 days.

A 2024 guideline recommends thatpatients with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis in low income countries should receive liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg as a single-dose, along with 14 days of flucytosine 25 mg/kg four times a day and fluconazole 1200 mg daily.

A trial randomized 814 patients with HIV disease and cryptococcal meningitis to this regimen or to a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg on day 1 plus 14 days of flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day) and fluconazole (1200 mg/day). The novel single dose amphotericin regimen was non-inferior with 24.8% mortality with the new regimen and 28.7% in the standard therapy group.It was also better tolerated with fewer adverse events.

Treat tuberculous meningitis presumed to be drug-susceptible with 2 months of daily INH (5 to 10 mg/kg/day, maximum 300 mg), rifampin (10 mg/kg/day, maximum 450 mg if < 50 kg, otherwise 600 mg), pyrazinamide (25 to 30 mg/kg/day, maximum daily dose 1500 mg if < 50 kg, otherwise 2000 mg), and either streptomycin (15 mg/kg/day in adults, 30 mg/kg/day in children, maximum 1000 mg), or ethambutol (15 to 20 mg/kg/day, 1600 maximum), followed by 7 to 10 months of INH and rifampin.
A trial randomized 520 HIV positive adults with tuberculous meningitis to either dexamethasone or placebo. There was no reduction in mortality overall or by prespecified subgroups with dexamethasone.
A small randomized controlled trial (n=40) found significantly better survival with the addition of adjunctive linelozid 1200 mg once daily to standard therapy.
There is insufficient evidence to compare maintenance versus restricted fluids for the outcome of mortality.

Children receiving maintenance fluids, compared with those whose fluids are restricted, have fewer seizures, are less likely to have spasticity and are less likely to have severe neurologic sequelae, although this evidence is of low quality. There are no RCTs in adults.
If patient is determined to have aseptic meningitis observation and symptomatic control is sufficient.
Therapeutic hypothermia is not beneficial in patients with severe bacterial meningitis and may be harmful.
As many as 1 in 4 hospitalized patients with bacterial meningitis die. C
Three clinical variables (hypotension, altered mental status, and seizure) predict adverse outcomes such as hearing loss, intellectual impairment, or other neurologic sequelae. C
Hypotension, altered mental status, and seizures predict a poor outcome. C
As many as 1 in 4 hospitalized patients with bacterial meningitis die.
Bacterial meningitis commonly results in hearing loss, focal neurologic deficits seizure disorder, severe ataxia, and memory disturbance.
Delay in starting antibiotics is associated with an increased risk of in-hospital mortality or prolonged neurologic deficit.

Three clinical variables (hypotension, altered mental status, and seizure) predict adverse outcomes such as hearing loss, intellectual impairment, or other neurologic sequelae. The absence of all of these was associated with a 9% risk. When one was present, the risk was 33% and when two were present the risk was 57%.
Up to 19% of patients who recover from pneumococcal meningitis have permanent hearing loss, intellectual impairment, or other serious neurological sequelae.
A repeat CSF analysis should be done if no improvement is seen after 48 hours of antibiotic therapy or if there is more than 8 days of fever.
While post infection hearing evaluation is recommended in children, there is no recommendation to routinely screen adults' hearing after meningitis.

In the elderly population, meningitis must be considered with any new neurologic sign, of which confusion is the most common. The elderly are 8 times more likely to present with confusion then the younger population.
In patients older than 60 years, N. meningitidis is rarely a cause of pyogenic meningitis. S. pneumoniae is the predominant organism (70%) followed by L. monocytogenes.

tr.td: PCN susceptible: penicillin or amoxicillin or ampicillin
Cephalosporin resistant: 1) vancomycin + rifampicin or 2) vancomycin + ceftriaxone or cefotaxime or 3) rifampicin + ceftriaxone or cefotaxine.
PCN susceptible: penicillin, amoxicillin, or ampicillin
Beta-lactamase negative: amoxicillin or ampicillin; if ampicillin resistant then ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus meropenem
Methicillin sensitive: flucloxacillin, nafcillin or oxacillin
Methicillin resistant: vancomycin; if vancomycin resistant linezolid
Ampicillin or amoxicillin; alternatives include trim-sulfa, moxifloxacin, meropenem and linezolid

Ceftriaxone (2 g q12 h) for 21 days
Amphotericin B (0.7-1.0 mg/kg/d) + flucytosine (100 mg/kg/d) until no clinical or laboratory signs of infection
Fluconazole (400 mg/d po) or itraconazole (400-600 mg/d po) indefinitely
